items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I brushed off what I remembered from all that and got involved in Scott Joplin specifically... I think that all piano music, not just jazz, not just Scott Joplin, but classical music in general, it should sound as though the performer is improvising it.

ctx.x: I believe one of your most recent recordings was a Gershwin collection? I’m curious as to, from a technical standpoint, what have you found was one of your most challenging prospects? Because when you record Scott Joplin, this is music that’s pretty much written out, yet it has to be played like it doesn’t sound like it’s written.

I think that all piano music, not just jazz, not just Scott Joplin, but classical music in general, it should sound as though the performer is improvising it. That’s what I think. And at its best, in my judgment, I can convince myself in an irrational way, that that is happening. And if you hear Mozart played that way, it sounds like the performer might be improvising it. We know they’re not. But there are aspects of performance that even people who are playing note for note understand. And it has to sound as…

How about your arranging career? What was some of your first experiences in arranging and was it difficult for you at that time, and did you learn this craft from someone else or was it kind of trial and error? © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: unexpected popularity of Scott Joplin from the movie “The Sting” and the various recordings, including my own

ctx.x: Well the Jelly Roll Morton album for Columbia was Sam Parkins’ idea, the producer. And he thought, and he got Columbia to think, that with the unexpected popularity of Scott Joplin from the movie “The Sting” and the various recordings, including my own, that perhaps Jelly Roll Morton would be the next on the list and that’s why we did that album. And we did it with several components. We did it like that record of “Grandpa’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

Spells” like that track of “Grandpa’s Spells” with a big band. It was my idea to make it like to a big concert marching band and that’s the way I arranged those things. We also did some smaller bands and we also did a couple of things as a trio with Joe Venuti — Panama Francis and Venuti and I. In fact Jelly Roll Morton did not become the next pop hit after Scott Joplin and I think the record has never paid for itself.
